clue.text: Go round a market, mostly in dense fog

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so one piece wraps the others

parts.note: go in the sense of energy or vigour, as is pep

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a souk is an Arab market; mostly drops its last letter

explanation.surface: A shopper does the rounds of a market while a thick fog hangs about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like a verb but is the noun meaning energy. A souk is a North African or Middle Eastern bazaar.
explanation.definitionFit: A pea-souper or pea soup is a thick yellowish London fog, named for its resemblance to the soup.

clue.text: Power lift gets acclaim

parts.note: P is the standard abbreviation for power
to lift something is to raise it

explanation.surface: A weightlifter's power lift earns applause from the crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Acclaim and praise are synonyms, both meaning public approval or admiration.

clue.text: A disease one got from a rodent

parts.note: taken as written
gout is a disease causing painful swollen joints
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone caught an illness from a rodent, as if from a rat.
explanation.definitionFit: The agouti is a long-legged burrowing rodent of Central and South America, related to the guinea pig.

clue.text: Flying separately, team's leader, not in touch with reality

parts.note: a traveller who flies separately is on a different aircraft

indicators.note: the leader of something is the one at the front, so only the opening letter of team is used

parts.note: the first letter of team

explanation.surface: A team member travels apart from the rest, with the captain seemingly lost in a daydream.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is itself a punning phrase: being on another plane means flying separately, and adding T turns plane into planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone said to be on another planet is dreamy or out of touch, an idiom for being detached from the real world.

clue.text: Head touring a Roman province

indicators.note: to tour something is to travel all around it, so one piece goes around the others

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head
taken as written
Latin was the language of the Romans, so Roman can mean Latin

explanation.surface: A leader goes on a tour of one of the provinces of the Roman Empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman province' reads as one phrase, but Roman belongs to the wordplay and province alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A palatinate is a territory ruled by a count palatine, such as the Rhine Palatinate, so it is a kind of province.

clue.text: Mounted bullfighter with pair doc treated

indicators.note: treated means processed or worked on, so the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An injured horseman of the bullring is patched up by a couple of doctors.
explanation.definitionFit: A picador is the bullfighter on horseback who weakens the bull with a lance before the matador's turn.

clue.text: Lick end of lollipop — superb

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of lollipop is used

parts.note: the last letter of lollipop
ace is slang for excellent

explanation.surface: A child licks the last of a lollipop and declares it superb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lick' looks like a verb about the lollipop, but it is the noun meaning speed, as in going at a fair lick.
explanation.definitionFit: A lick is informal for a speed of movement, so it can stand for pace.

clue.text: A game of chess where pin is disastrous

indicators.note: a disastrous arrangement has gone badly wrong, so the letters are thrown into a different order

parts.note: the first part of the fodder
taken as written, the rest of the fodder

explanation.surface: A chess game in which getting a piece pinned proves catastrophic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' sits between fodder and indicator and reads like a link, but its letters are needed in the anagram. A pin in chess traps a piece in front of a more valuable one.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinese whispers is a party game in which a message passed along a line gets garbled, known in the US as telephone.

clue.text: Evil toad, awfully fit

indicators.note: awfully means very badly, so the letters come out badly arranged

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A wicked toad is remarkably healthy, as if describing a fairy-tale villain.
explanation.definitionFit: To dovetail is to fit together neatly, from the interlocking woodworking joint of the same name.

clue.text: Artist associated with Rhode Island draws freaks

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the standard crossword artist
the postal abbreviation for the US state
draws in games are ties

explanation.surface: An artist linked to an American state sketches bizarre figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draws' looks like what an artist does, but it is the noun meaning drawn matches.
explanation.definitionFit: A freak can be an unusual or abnormal occurrence, so freaks are oddities or rarities.

clue.text: A gypsy with a distinctive smell

parts.note: taken as written
the Roma are the Romani people, traditionally called gypsies

explanation.surface: A travelling gypsy carries an unmistakable scent.
explanation.definitionFit: An aroma is a characteristic and usually pleasant odour, such as that of coffee or baking.

clue.text: Literary hero found in lake in Virginia close to Bridgewater

parts.note: loch is the Scottish word for a lake
taken as written
the abbreviation for the US state

indicators.note: the close of a word is where it ends, so only the last letter of Bridgewater is taken

parts.note: the final letter of Bridgewater

explanation.surface: A storybook hero turns up at a lake in Virginia not far from a town called Bridgewater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' reads as part of the location phrase but supplies its own two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Young Lochinvar is the dashing knight of a ballad in Walter Scott's poem Marmion, who rides off with his love.

clue.text: Start out on a journey with group, by the side of Scottish river

parts.note: a set is a group of things
the Forth flows into the Firth of Forth at Edinburgh

explanation.surface: A party begins a trip together along the banks of a Scottish river.
explanation.definitionFit: To set forth is an old-fashioned phrasal verb for departing, beginning a journey.

clue.text: Be up to some criminal activity then make off furtively

parts.note: taken as written
someone at it is busy doing something, often mischief or crime

explanation.surface: A crook is up to no good and then sneaks away.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat it is a slang command or idiom meaning go away quickly, like scram or clear off.

clue.text: Welsh party dry? I clam up, perplexed

indicators.note: perplexed means confused, so the letters are muddled into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A puzzled member of a Welsh political party, asked if it is teetotal, goes silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dry' suggests a temperance question, but it is just fodder letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaid Cymru, Welsh for Party of Wales, is the Welsh nationalist political party.

clue.text: A row of policemen, inadequate down by railway track

parts.note: a thin excuse is an inadequate one
feeling down is feeling blue
a railway line is the track

explanation.surface: A cordon of officers, too sparse to do the job, stands beside the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down' could be a direction or a crossword clue label; here it means sad.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin blue line is an idiom for the police as the barrier between order and chaos, from their blue uniforms.

clue.text: Inflict a heavy defeat upon a large number — fixed race

parts.note: a mass is a large number of things

indicators.note: a fixed race has been rigged, so its letters are rigged into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A crowd of punters is thrashed when the race turns out to be rigged.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase, so the answer is the verb, as in the team was massacred.
explanation.definitionFit: To massacre an opponent is informal for beating them overwhelmingly, extended from the sense of slaughter.

clue.text: A female, graceful and wealthy

parts.note: taken as written
F is the standard abbreviation for female
fluent movement is smooth and graceful

explanation.surface: A description of a woman who is elegant and rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluent means having plenty of money, a straightforward synonym of rich.

clue.text: Immediately before any serious study took place

definitions.text: Immediately before any serious study took place

parts.words: Immediately before any serious study took place
parts.note: surface reading: something happening right before research or revision began

parts.words: Immediately before any serious study took place
parts.note: setter's reading: on the first glance, before anything was examined closely, as when falling in love instantly

explanation.walkthrough: 'study' suggests academic work, but it means looking at something, so the phrase describes the very first look.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a judgment or feeling formed on first seeing something, with no closer examination yet.

clue.text: Ian leaving US state with a girl

indicators.note: when someone is leaving they depart, so those letters go out of the longer word

parts.note: the southern US state
the name, taken as written, removed from the state

explanation.surface: A man named Ian departs from an American state in the company of a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The name to remove sits whole in the middle of the state, and the letters either side simply close up.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisa is a female first name, so it is an example of a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: Express agreement when told to go

parts.note: as can mean when, as in as I arrived
someone told to go has been sent away

explanation.surface: Someone nods along on being ordered to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'told' tempts a solver to hear a homophone of ascent, but it is plain wordplay: the answer is spelt as built.
explanation.definitionFit: To assent is a formal verb meaning to agree or give approval to a proposal.

clue.text: Very good Dutch painter is alone

parts.note: so means very, as in so tired
Sir Peter Lely, Dutch-born portrait painter at the court of Charles II

explanation.surface: A fine Netherlandish artist works in solitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good' is a compliment to the painter rather than a separate piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Solely and alone both mean only, excluding anyone else, as in he alone or he solely is responsible.

clue.text: Son is cross, failing to identify cutters

indicators.note: failing means breaking down, so the letters break up and re-form

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boy is annoyed at being unable to tell which blades are which.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like the son's mood, but its letters go into the mix with S and IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Scissors are a cutting tool, so they can be called cutters.

clue.text: One famous golfer turned up in Anglesey, say

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means read from bottom to top, so the golfer's name runs backwards

parts.note: Ernie Els, South African major champion

explanation.surface: A celebrated golfer appeared at a tournament on a Welsh island.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglesey is an island off north-west Wales, so it is an example of an isle, flagged by say.

clue.text: G-man chose ridiculous dress

indicators.note: ridiculous suggests something absurd or nonsensical, so the letters are put into a nonsensical order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An FBI agent picked out an absurd frock, perhaps for an undercover job.
explanation.walkthrough: A G-man is American slang for an FBI agent; here it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheongsam is a close-fitting Chinese dress with a high collar and slit skirt, also called a qipao.

clue.text: Select piece of escalope, low in calories

indicators.note: a piece is a small part, here just the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the first letter of escalope
lite is the marketing spelling for low-calorie food

explanation.surface: Choose a bit of the escalope, a diet-friendly option.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Select' looks like an instruction to pick, but it is the adjective meaning choice. An escalope is a thin slice of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: The elite are the select few, the best or most privileged of a group.

clue.text: Call of wren tit learned

indicators.note: of here means made from part of, so the letters come from within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A wren learns the song of a tit, as a birdwatcher might note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call' looks like a birdsong, but it is the verb meaning to name.
explanation.definitionFit: To entitle a book or work is to give it a name, so it means to call.

clue.text: Sup bubbly, before biting mushroom

indicators.note: bubbly suggests fizzing and churning, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: the letters to rearrange
a tart remark is sharp or biting

explanation.surface: Drink champagne before eating a mushroom, as at a dinner party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bubbly' and 'mushroom' both suggest food and drink, but mushroom is a noun for a person who shoots up suddenly in status.
explanation.definitionFit: Mushroom is an old term for an upstart, someone who has risen suddenly to wealth or importance, like a fungus overnight.
